name: David Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the disability benefit review team at the regional processing centre, the big grey building by the ring road. Most of the day I'm on the phone with claimants or reading through doctors' letters and deciding what evidence we still need. I'm eighteen months in and still the one asking the senior caseworkers what a form means. I like the calls where you can hear someone relax because you actually listened.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya, who teaches Year 4 at the primary school round the corner. We're saving for a house, and my granddad left me some money a couple of years ago, so we're in a better spot than most of my mates. I've just started training as a union rep, which mostly means sitting in on grievance meetings and taking notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. We've had a pilot tool for summarising medical letters since last year, and it's useful about half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: handy for the boring bits, not a revolution. In the union meetings I'd say good, now we can talk about staffing instead of robots. Online I probably wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I use the summary tool now and then when the letter's twelve pages of a consultant's handwriting scanned sideways. If that's as far as it goes, I keep learning the job the slow way, which is how you actually get good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, basically. I'd use the letter tool when it helps and check everything it says. I'd keep putting six hundred a month into the house fund and keep up the union rep training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The job's secure, the pay's decent for a junior, and there are three other benefit centres within a bus ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check everything the tool says. Has it ever got something wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summary tool once told me a claimant could walk two hundred metres when the letter said twenty. One zero. If I hadn't read the original, that man would have lost his mobility payment. So I trust it the way you trust a new colleague, which is not much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you two buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably next spring. Priya wants a garden, I want to be near the bus route, and we'd both like to stop paying someone else's mortgage. Nothing in this picture changes that.

say: AI is handy for the **boring bits**, not a revolution.
Now the union can talk about **staffing levels** instead of robots.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I learn the job the slow, proper way.
I'll use the **summary tool** only on the worst scanned letters.
do: Keep **checking every summary** against the original doctor's letter.
Put **£600 a month** into the house fund as now.
Finish the **union rep training** this year.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **relieved** about the job and the house plan.
S0.quote: The summary tool once told me a claimant could walk two hundred metres when the letter said twenty.
fieldNote: He uses AI **now and then** but treats it like an untested colleague.
A **single missing zero** shapes his whole trust in the tool.
**House plans** with his partner carry on untouched in this world.

steps.text: Keep checking every AI letter summary against the original
Buy a house with Priya next spring as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the review team in a nutshell. Reading evidence, writing decisions, answering calls: all thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a deal before the tools arrive, not after. At work that's my rep hat: no compulsory redundancies, retraining for anyone moved off cases, and a human signs every decision. Online I'd keep it calm and factual, because people are scared of benefits being decided by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, juniors like me are the cheap ones to lose. They won't sack us, they'll just stop hiring, and the next round of temporary contracts won't be renewed. I'm permanent, so I'm probably fine for a couple of years, but I'm not good enough yet to be the person who checks the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on the pilot team properly, so I'm one of the people who knows how the tools fail. I'd push the union for a written agreement within six months. And Priya and I would put the house off a year and keep the deposit in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like I'd be learning the job and watching it get smaller at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put the house off if your savings are strong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because once you've got a mortgage, you take whatever deal they offer. With the deposit still in the bank, I can say no to a bad transfer. Priya agreed, though she'd rather not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How bad would losing the job be, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. My granddad's money and our savings would carry us a long time. It's the career I'm worried about, not the rent.

say: We need a **union deal** before the tools arrive, not after.
A **human signs every decision** on someone's disability benefit.
think: Juniors are **cheap to lose**: no sackings, just no new hires.
I'm not yet good enough to be the one who **checks the machine**.
do: Join the **AI pilot team** to learn how the tools fail.
Push for a **written union agreement** within six months.
**Delay the house** a year and keep the deposit banked.
feel: **Anxious**, learning the job while it **gets smaller**.
S1.quote: Once you've got a mortgage, you take whatever deal they offer.
fieldNote: He moves **once it's proven**: the pilot team is his careful step in.
His union role turns worry into a **concrete ask**.
Money isn't the fear; the **shrinking career** is.

steps.text: Join the AI pilot team on the disability review floor
Push for a written no-redundancy agreement within six months
Delay the house purchase a year and keep the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's two years. I'd barely have finished my rep training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the government has to slow this down in public services. Benefits are a promise from the state to people, and you can't hand that to a machine in two years. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone. Not just mine, the whole review team. Reading letters and deciding is exactly what that card describes, and I'm not even the best at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first months to push for a proper redundancy and retraining package, because that's what the union can still win. Then I'd retrain for something hands-on with people, maybe a support worker or something in Priya's school, like a teaching assistant. The robots come three years after, so that's at least some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd be lying awake doing sums and then remembering the sums aren't the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's job is more hands-on than mine, with thirty kids in a room. She'd probably last longer. I'd hate being the one leaning on her, even with the money from my granddad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the house still happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want the house, eventually. But not in 2028, not with two incomes that could both be wobbling by 2031.

say: Government must **slow this down** in public services.
Benefits are a **promise from the state**, not a machine's job.
think: The **whole review team** is gone, not just me.
**Reading letters and deciding** is exactly what AGI does.
do: Fight for a **retraining package** through the union first.
Retrain as a **support worker** or teaching assistant.
**Shelve the house** until both jobs look steady.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake on sums that **aren't the problem**.
S2.quote: Benefits are a promise from the state to people, and you can't hand that to a machine in two years.
fieldNote: He sees his **whole team** lost, not just himself.
He looks to **hands-on people work**, using the three-year robot gap.
He dislikes the idea of **leaning on his partner**.

steps.text: Organise for a union retraining and redundancy package
Retrain as a teaching assistant or support worker
Shelve the house purchase until both jobs look steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to see it coming but not enough to stop it. It's like the slow one, only with an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to plan, and I'd say it to management directly as a rep. Every caseworker should get a retraining offer with their name on it. I'd also tell my mates to stop pretending it's years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get two or three good years on the review team and then I'd need to be somewhere else. The extra three years give me time to get properly good at advising people, which I'm not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time welfare rights advice course, so I can work at the advice centre on the high street, helping people challenge decisions. I'd use the AI tools more at work, so I'm not a stranger to them. Priya and I would buy a smaller house than planned and keep more back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real, but I'd have my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why welfare rights advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will need someone on their side when a machine turns them down. The advice centre has a waiting list of six weeks now. I don't think that shrinks just because the decisions get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI could give advice too, though. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's true, it could. But a person sitting next to you while you appeal still matters. I'd bet five years on that, not my whole life.

say: This is **the moment to plan**, not to pretend.
Every caseworker deserves a **named retraining offer**.
I'd tell my mates to **stop pretending** it's years away.
think: I've got **two or three** good years before I must move.
The extra time lets me get **good at advising**.
do: Start a **welfare rights course** part-time in the first year.
**Use AI tools more** at work to stay familiar.
**Buy a smaller house** and keep more savings back.
feel: **Anxious**, but with my **hands on** the wheel.
S3.quote: People will need someone on their side when a machine turns them down.
fieldNote: Five years turns his alarm into a **plan with dates**.
He moves from deciding claims to **fighting decisions**, a side switch.
He'd now **use AI more**, a steady person's measured shift.

steps.text: Start a part-time welfare rights advice course next year
Use the AI letter tools daily on review cases
Buy a smaller house than planned with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to do something completely new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so let's use it properly: training budgets, a plan for every public service. I'd probably be a bit boring about it at parties. People would stop asking me about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job looks safe for a good few years. I'd watch it change around me, but I wouldn't lose sleep yet. The worry is more for the claimants and for the older staff who've got less time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next spring as planned. I'd keep working and get good at the casework and the AI tools as they come in. Around year four or five, I'd look at moving to the advice centre or a union job full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just aware the ground is moving under the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What job would you want at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably full-time organising for the union, honestly. Someone will have to bargain for people like me when the end point comes. I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dorothy on my team, who's fifty-eight. She'd be at retirement by 2036, so maybe she's fine. The people in their forties with kids are the ones I'd worry about.

say: We have **a decade**, so use it: training budgets for every service.
I'd be **boring at parties** about this.
think: My job looks **safe for years**, so I won't lose sleep yet.
I worry more for **colleagues in their forties** with kids.
do: **Buy the house** next spring as planned.
**Learn the AI tools** as they arrive in the review team.
Aim for a **full-time union job** by year five.
S4.quote: Someone will have to bargain for people like me when the end point comes. I'd like to be that person.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **keep life plans** and still prepare.
His **union ambition** becomes a real career idea.
His worry shifts outward to **mid-career colleagues**.

steps.text: Buy the house with Priya next spring as planned
Learn each new AI tool as the review team gets it
Apply for a full-time union organiser job by year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Two years isn't time for a union to win anything, and it isn't time for me to get good at anything new. What would help is a guaranteed retraining place for every public sector worker whose job goes, paid and with a salary while you do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether we trust the people making these decisions. I trust my team leader. I don't trust the department to choose the cheapest tool and call it progress. If the people at the top were honest about the timeline, a lot of us could plan instead of panic.

headlineQuote: If the people at the top were honest about the timeline, a lot of us could plan instead of panic.
portrait: A **27-year-old disability benefit reviewer** at a regional centre, eighteen months in and still learning.
He uses an AI letter tool **now and then** and checks it after it once dropped a zero.
**Savings and an inheritance** make the career, not the rent, his real worry.
As a **trainee union rep**, he answers every scenario by bargaining for retraining and human sign-off.
With more time he plans **welfare rights advice** or union work, and the house goes ahead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for unions or for him to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining place** for every public worker whose job goes.
**Honest timelines** from the people at the top so staff can plan.
